newsitem.title: FRANCE: Siege of French bank enters fourth day.
newsitem.headline: Siege of French bank enters fourth day.

text.p: Senior officials of the Credit Foncier bank began a fourth day as hostages of their angry employees on Monday in a standoff with the French government over job security and the bank's fate.
Several hundred employees occupying its plush Paris headquarters said the bank would open for business as usual even as they continued to bar the captive executives from leaving.
The atmosphere inside the bank was more like that of a church picnic than an armed camp and bank governor Jerome Meysonnier, a hostage, warned against dramatising his plight.
Many employees had their children with them in the marble lobby as teams took turns preparing food, standing guard and debating strategy.

The workers even allowed Meysonnier to hold a news conference in the board room, where he refused to criticise the staff and held out hopes for a solution that would get around a government plan to dismantle the bank, one of France's oldest.
The standoff is shaping up as a new test for the government of Prime Minister Alain Juppe, pursuing a tight spending policy in the run-up to a single European currency.

The government has repeatedly bowed to union protests in the past, raising doubts whether it can stay the course with its austerity budget. It has said it would take five billion francs ($900 million) to keep Credit Foncier in one piece.

The affair also highlighted close ties between the state and the banking sector, as staff and shareholders suspected an effort to sink the bank and close an embarrassing saga of losses in which the state was involved.
Finance Minister Jean Arthuis proposed spinning off Credit Foncier's housing loans and commercial business to co-operatively run Credit Immobilier, which has pledged to take 1,500 staff.
The rest of the bank would be wound down, raising the spectre of job losses among the 3,300 people now on the payroll.
Meysonnier, though appointed by the government, has been holding out the possibility of a venture with a rescue partner rather than the partial takeover proposed by Arthuis.

Union leaders hailed his remarks as a step in the right direction. They said he appeared to be acting as a go-between between union leaders and the government, an impression strengthened when Arthuis called him by portable telephone during his news conference.

Credit Foncier manages billions of bonds in French debt and operates low-cost housing loans on behalf of the state. The 145-year-old private bank ran into deep trouble last year after posting a 10.8 billion franc ($2.0 billion) 1995 loss.
